questions.question_text: How many commissioners serve on the Wyoming Real Estate Commission?
questions.explanation: The Wyoming Real Estate Commission (WREC) is composed of 5 members appointed by the Governor with Senate consent. This relatively small commission size reflects Wyoming's smaller population while still providing adequate oversight of the real estate profession.

questions.question_text: The Governor is filling one of the WREC seats reserved for real estate licensees. The nominee has been licensed and active in Wyoming for 3 years. Does the nominee qualify for that seat?
questions.correct_answer: No, that seat requires 5 years of Wyoming licensed experience
distractors: Yes, any actively licensed Wyoming salesperson or broker qualifies
Yes, provided the Wyoming Senate confirms the nominee
No, that seat requires 10 years of Wyoming licensed experience
questions.explanation: W.S. 33-28-105(a) provides that "not less than three (3) or more than four (4) of the membership shall have been engaged in business as a licensee in Wyoming for at least five (5) years immediately preceding appointment." A nominee with only 3 years does not qualify for one of those licensee seats, and Senate confirmation cannot cure a statutory qualification defect. Two details matter: the experience must be Wyoming experience, and it must fall in the 5 years immediately preceding appointment. Also note the 5-year rule reaches only the 3 to 4 licensee seats - because no more than four members may be 5-year licensees, at least one of the five seats must always go to someone who is not.

questions.question_text: Which body must consent to the Governor's appointments to WREC?
questions.explanation: Under W.S. 33-28-105(a) the five commissioners are "appointed by the governor with the advice and consent of the senate." Senate confirmation is a legislative check on the executive appointment. Related qualifications from the same subsection: each commissioner must be a Wyoming citizen, no more than one commissioner may be appointed from the same county at a time, terms run 3 years, and no member may succeed himself for more than one full term. The Governor may remove a commissioner as provided in W.S. 9-1-202.

questions.question_text: A newly constituted WREC has 2 active licensees and 3 public members. Does this composition comply with Wyoming law?
questions.correct_answer: No, 3 to 4 members must be active licensees
distractors: Yes, any mix of members is acceptable
Yes, a public member majority is required
No, all 5 members must be licensees
questions.explanation: Wyoming law mandates that 3 to 4 of the 5 WREC commissioners must be active real estate licensees with at least 5 years of experience. Having only 2 licensees violates this composition requirement and would need to be corrected.

questions.question_text: At minimum, how many of the five WREC commissioners must have been engaged in business as a Wyoming real estate licensee for the 5 years immediately preceding appointment?
questions.explanation: W.S. 33-28-105(a): "Not less than three (3) or more than four (4) of the membership shall have been engaged in business as a licensee in Wyoming for at least five (5) years immediately preceding appointment." Three is the floor and four is the ceiling, so at least one of the five seats must always be filled by someone who is not a 5-year Wyoming licensee. Note the statute tests prior business experience as a licensee in the 5 years before appointment, not whether the member holds an active license while serving.

questions.question_text: WREC receives a consumer complaint about a licensee's advertising. What investigative authority does the commission have?
questions.correct_answer: It may investigate and examine broker records
distractors: It must refer the matter to local police
It can only investigate if the broker consents
It must wait for a court order to investigate
questions.explanation: W.S. 33-28-111(a) empowers the commission to "upon a written sworn complaint or ... upon its own motion investigate the actions of any licensee conducting real estate advertising, self promotion as a licensee or real estate activity" in Wyoming, and misleading or inaccurate advertising is a ground for discipline under W.S. 33-28-111(a)(vi). A licensee who fails "to provide information requested by the Commission relative to a complaint, investigation, or audit" violates WREC Rules ch. 6 s. 1(a)(x). No broker consent and no court order is needed. One wrinkle: the commission's duty to investigate is mandatory only on a written sworn complaint, and WREC Rules ch. 8 s. 2(a) requires a sworn written complaint to initiate a formal disciplinary action - an unsworn consumer tip is pursued on the commission's own motion.

questions.question_text: A WREC investigator arrives at a brokerage unannounced requesting to audit the trust account. Can the broker refuse?
questions.correct_answer: No, WREC can audit trust accounts at any time
distractors: Yes, WREC must give 30 days written notice
Yes, unless WREC has a search warrant
Yes, unless the commission first opens a formal complaint file
questions.explanation: W.S. 33-28-122(a)(iii) requires every responsible broker to "permit the commission or its representative to examine the responsible broker's trust accounting records," and WREC Rules ch. 5 s. 2 provides that "the Commission may audit the Responsible Broker's trust or escrow account records to assure compliance with Commission rules and statutes." Neither imposes an advance-notice, warrant, or business-hours condition, so the broker cannot refuse. Refusing is separately sanctionable: WREC Rules ch. 6 s. 1(a)(x) covers failing to provide information requested relative to a complaint, investigation, or audit. Brokers must keep the underlying records for at least 2 years under W.S. 33-28-123.

questions.question_text: Which of the following WREC powers allows it to create binding regulations for licensees?
questions.explanation: WREC possesses rulemaking authority, which allows it to promulgate rules and regulations that carry the force of law for all licensees. These rules supplement the Wyoming Real Estate License Act and provide detailed operational standards for the profession.

questions.question_text: WREC notices irregularities in a broker's MLS activity even though no complaint has been filed. Can WREC open an investigation?
distractors: No, a consumer must file a complaint first
No, only the Attorney General can initiate
Yes, but only with a court order
questions.explanation: WREC has the power to self-initiate investigations without receiving a formal complaint. When the commission identifies potential violations through its own monitoring, it may independently open and conduct an investigation to protect the public.

questions.question_text: A broker claims WREC has no authority to review his transaction files because no one has filed a complaint against him. Is the broker correct?
questions.correct_answer: No, WREC may investigate on its own motion
distractors: Yes, transaction files are private absent a complaint
Yes, WREC must first obtain a subpoena
No, but only for files less than 1 year old
questions.explanation: W.S. 33-28-111(a) lets the commission act "upon a written sworn complaint or ... upon its own motion," so no outside complaint is required. Once an investigation or audit is open, a licensee who unreasonably fails "to produce documents of record in his possession or under his control concerning any real estate transaction under investigation by the commission" violates W.S. 33-28-111(a)(xii), and WREC Rules ch. 6 s. 1(a)(x) covers failing to provide information relative to a complaint, investigation, or audit. Trust accounting records are separately open to examination under W.S. 33-28-122(a)(iii). The 1-year option fails because W.S. 33-28-123 requires records be kept at least 2 years, and the subpoena option fails because chapter 28 gives the commission no subpoena power - that authority belongs to the hearing officer in a contested case under W.S. 33-28-113(b).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a disciplinary sanction available to WREC?
questions.explanation: WREC may revoke a license under W.S. 33-28-111(a). WREC Rules ch. 6 s. 1 gives the complete menu: disciplinary action "includes an administrative fine, censure, probation, suspension, or revocation, including a combination thereof." The administrative fine is capped at $2,500 for each separate offense, and under W.S. 33-28-111(c) fines are paid to the public school fund of the county where the violation occurred. WREC cannot prosecute crimes, impose jail, or award damages - those are judicial functions. Criminal charges for unlicensed activity are brought in court under W.S. 33-28-114, and injunctions are sought by the attorney general or district attorney under W.S. 33-28-112.

questions.question_text: A salesperson commits a first-time minor advertising violation. Which sanction is WREC MOST likely to impose?
questions.explanation: Censure is WREC's entry-level sanction, and W.S. 33-28-111(a) also authorizes an administrative fine "not to exceed two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500.00) for each separate offense." Advertising that is misleading or inaccurate in a material matter is a ground under W.S. 33-28-111(a)(vi). Revocation is reserved for serious or repeated misconduct, WREC cannot charge crimes, and no permanent ban exists. Censures still carry weight: receiving more than three censures within a 2-year period is itself a ground for discipline under W.S. 33-28-111(a)(xxxiii). Note that mandatory education is not one of the enumerated sanctions in WREC Rules ch. 6 s. 1 - it reaches a licensee only as a term of probation or as conditional settlement terms under WREC Rules ch. 8 s. 4(c)(iii).

questions.question_text: A licensee has been found guilty of repeated trust account violations. WREC places the licensee on probation with conditions. What additional sanctions could WREC also impose?
questions.correct_answer: An administrative fine of up to $2,500 per offense
distractors: Only probation may be imposed at one time
questions.explanation: WREC Rules ch. 6 s. 1 expressly permits stacking: disciplinary action "includes an administrative fine, censure, probation, suspension, or revocation, including a combination thereof." W.S. 33-28-111(a) authorizes an administrative fine "not to exceed two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500.00) for each separate offense" alongside censure, probation, suspension or revocation, so probation is not exclusive. Commingling and failing to keep others' funds in an escrow or trust account are grounds under W.S. 33-28-111(a)(xiv) and (a)(xxvi). WREC cannot impose jail - that requires a criminal conviction under W.S. 33-28-114 - and there is no automatic federal referral. Fines collected go to the public school fund of the county where the violation occurred, per W.S. 33-28-111(c).

questions.question_text: WREC suspends a broker's license for 6 months. During the suspension, the broker continues to conduct real estate transactions. What is the likely consequence?
distractors: A warning letter is the maximum action
questions.explanation: Practicing while suspended violates W.S. 33-28-111(a)(ii) - violation of the act or any rule of the commission - and WREC Rules ch. 6 s. 2(a) confirms that a licensee whose license is suspended or revoked may not perform any real estate activity. WREC can escalate to revocation and add an administrative fine of up to $2,500 for each separate offense under W.S. 33-28-111(a). Separately, performing real estate activity without a valid license is a misdemeanor under W.S. 33-28-114(a), punishable by a fine of up to $2,500 or up to 6 months in county jail, rising to $5,000 or 1 year for a subsequent violation - but that charge is brought by a prosecutor in court, not by WREC.

questions.question_text: Which disciplinary action allows a licensee to keep practicing while meeting specific conditions set by WREC?
questions.explanation: Probation allows a licensee to continue practicing under specific conditions imposed by WREC. Unlike suspension, which prohibits practice entirely, or revocation, which terminates the license, probation provides a middle-ground sanction while ensuring compliance through oversight.
